title: Copying DNA, almost perfectly
hook: Each cycle copies a little less than perfectly. How far behind after 30 cycles?

doesNotKnow: that a slightly lower per-cycle factor compounds into a large shortfall

misconception: 90% efficient copying gives about 90% of the perfect result.
objective: The learner can explain that a x1.9 cycle instead of x2 is 95% of perfect, and 0.95 multiplied over 30 cycles leaves about 21% of the perfect count.

claims.text: In the exponential phase of PCR each cycle roughly doubles the number of DNA copies; real efficiency is below 100%.
claims.source: Saiki et al., Science 239, 1988 (PCR); Kubista et al., Molecular Aspects of Medicine 27, 2006 (efficiency in real-time PCR).

claims.text: After 30 cycles, a perfect doubling gives 2^30 = 1.07 billion copies from one molecule; at x1.9 per cycle it gives 1.9^30 = 230 million, which is 21% of perfect.
claims.source: Computed in Demo.tsx from count(e, c) = (1 + e/100)^c; node check: 1.9^30 = 230,466,618; 2^30 = 1,073,741,824; ratio 0.2146. Other stage values: 80% gives 45.5 million (4%), 95% gives 502 million (47%).

claims.text: Model (stated on the stage): one starting molecule, a fixed efficiency every cycle, no plateau. A x1.9 cycle is 0.95 of a perfect cycle, and 0.95 multiplied 30 times is 0.21.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx; brief life #44. Real PCR plateaus as reagents run out (Kubista et al. 2006). 0.95^30 = 0.2146.

recall.question: A copying process should double each cycle but only manages x1.9. After 30 cycles, the result is closest to what share of the perfect count?
recall.why: Each cycle is 95% of perfect, and that shortfall multiplies every cycle: 0.95^30 is about 0.21.
